title: Follow the GPUs: How a Regulated Fortune 100 Serves Customers When No Single Cloud Has Enough
tldr: GEICO runs a hybrid cloud fabric (flat L3 network, identical clusters, SPIFFE/SPIRE identity, Istio and Cilium) that makes moving a workload between Azure and AWS just a redeploy. They built a probe tool that measured GPU availability across providers for four weeks and found multi-region helps only for scarce SKUs, and propose a capacity booking agent since autoscalers never buy capacity.

key_points.text: Takeaways first: for current single-GPU SKUs right now, support multi-region; for 8-GPU flagship nodes, book ahead; and someone still has to do the booking, because autoscalers will not.
The fabric was built for other reasons: four nines across 50 states, replacing about a thousand team-owned clusters and over a million firewall rules with a provider-agnostic zero-trust overlay.

Foundation: one flat L3 network with routable node and pod IPs across providers; identical clusters from immutable hardened images, kubeadm and Ansible, with components on the same versions and delivered by GitOps.
SPIRE issues SPIFFE IDs and short-lived SVIDs from attested evidence; Istio sidecars enforce mTLS with certs from the SPIRE agent; Cilium enforces deny-by-default L3/L4 policy.
Teams describe apps and their communication; the platform generates Cilium and Istio policy, with automatic approval for most rules and human review for risky ones.

The control plane runs active-active in three regions on Cassandra, which also backs a SPIRE fork with a pluggable datastore proposed upstream; Kafka is the fleet bus, and a mesh agent syncs endpoints and policy to each cluster.
Because identity and rules attach to what a workload is, not where it runs, moving from Azure to AWS is a redeploy with the same global name and no client changes.
Providers now offer bookable capacity (e.g. AWS capacity blocks, up to 8 weeks out, paid up front, no refunds) between on-demand and reserved; Karpenter will use a reservation ID but never buys one.

The 'follow the GPUs' tool doubles its GPU request until refused, with Blackbox Exporter-style probe config, free probes (spot score and price) and billable catch-and-release probes, telemetry in S3/Blob queried with DuckDB, and a scheduled sweeper as an emergency brake.

Results: small single-GPU SKUs gain nothing from multi-region, L40S gains about 5%, sparse RTX Pro 6000 gains a lot, and B200 is not available on demand but multi-region raises odds of getting one within two days.

Q&A: multi-cluster autoscaling approaches still just wait and retry when refused; Azure model-as-a-service by data zone plus an AI gateway can soften shortages; NVIDIA Dynamo intent CRs are scoped to one cluster.

numbers.text: About 1,000 Kubernetes clusters and over 1 million firewall rules in the old model.
Control plane runs in three regions, all active.
Inference cost for the same capability drops roughly 10x per year (cited from Guido Appenzeller), so 100x in two years.
Capacity can be booked up to 8 weeks ahead.
A catch-and-release probe took about 30 seconds to 2 minutes per VM.
Ran about four weeks across every zone of three AWS regions and nine Azure regions, collecting about 50,000 samples.
L40S: about 5% improvement from multi-region; RTX Pro 6000: from about 45% to 70-75%.
B200: chance of getting capacity within two days rose from about 65% to 88%.

open_gaps.text: No autoscaler books capacity; when the provider says no they can only wait and retry. GEICO proposes a booking agent with an interface for need, timing and budget, informed by history.
The booking agent and multi-cluster placement layer do not exist yet; they are still checking whether it would help.
Data gravity constrains where many workloads can run.
Securing agents with workload identity is unsolved; sidecar credential injection is the direction, but no full answer yet.

opportunities.text: Run GEICO's shared probe tool in your own accounts to measure GPU SKU availability by region before committing to multi-region.
Help define the interface for a GPU capacity booking agent that reserves capacity just before pods go pending.
Review the SPIRE pluggable datastore proposal and the Cassandra-backed implementation.
Identity-based (SPIFFE) network policy that lets workloads move across clouds without rewriting rules.
